title: Gitxsan hereditary chiefs call for halt to rail cargo as diesel leaks from train derailment along river in B.C.
summary: A second landslide and train derailment into the Skeena River in eight months has reignited calls by the Gitxsan Huwilp Government to immediately stop train hauling in the vicinity of its traditional…

image.caption: CN says initial information suggests the Nov. 17 derailment near Terrace, B.C., was caused by a rockslide. (Carl J. Reibin)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A second landslide and train derailment into the Skeena River in eight months has reignited calls by the Gitxsan Huwilp Government to immediately stop train hauling in the vicinity of its traditional territory.
2nd train derailment in northwest B.C in 8 months threatens food security, says Gitxsan Huwilp Government
Two people were taken to hospital on Tuesday after a Canadian National Railway train carrying forestry products went off the tracks due to a rockslide.
Two locomotives and five railcars carrying multiple containers of forest products derailed approximately 17 kilometres west of Terrace, B.C.
Images from the scene showed several cars off the track, with multiple containers in the water.
2 CN Rail employees injured after train derails near Terrace
CN said diesel has leaked from a locomotive, and crews are working to contain the spill and repair the route. The two employees have since been released from hospital.

It's the second spill recorded in the area this year, after a mudslide derailed grain cars along the Skeena during extreme weather in March, resulting in 7,949 litres of diesel being released, 3,421 of which were "unaccounted for," according to the B.C. government's spill response page.

items: 2 hospitalized after CN Rail train derails into Skeena River near Terrace, B.C.

blocks.text: Prior to that incident, there were no major spill reports along the rail line from Terrace to Prince Rupert over the past decade.

But with two events in such a close timespan, Simogyet Skogam'Lahkx Toby Howard said Tuesday’s incident shows a derailment remains "a clear and present danger" to the food security of the Gitxsan people.
A CN Rail train is seen partially spilled into the Skeena River in northwest B.C. in this photo provided by the Gitxsan Huwilp Government on March 17, 2026. (Gitxsan Huwilp Government)
"The fish in the Skeena feed the eagles, the seals and importantly the Gitxsan people," he said in a release.
"People were transported to hospital, and another train is in the Skeena River — train hauling is dangerous and must stop immediately."
Call for rail moratorium in northwest
Howard added that he feels the Ministry of Transportation downplays the derailments and the possibility of future disasters.
He said hauling needs to stop until the route from Burns Lake to Prince Rupert is inspected and safety can be guaranteed.
"A 103-year-old track has created dangerous conditions for the rail system in our territory," he said.
"Gitxsan Hereditary Chiefs have offered their assistance in identifying the areas of most vulnerability on the line but The Ministry of Transportation has dismissed us."
The B.C. government and related ministries have not commented on the incident prior to the swearing-in of premier designate Lorne Doerkson, instead directing media to its spill response page.
It says "an oil sheen appears to extend approximately 1.3 km downstream," adding that the "quantity of product released remains unconfirmed."

The province considers diesel a "non-persistent oil" as it disperses and evaporates more readily than crude oil. However, it notes diesel can still pose a risk to marine animals and birds if they come into contact with a slick.
In a statement, CN said crews and specialized equipment are on site and recovery operations are underway.
The company is working to contain the spill, remove derailed equipment and prepare for track repairs.
Environmental response measures are in place in the Skeena River to minimize impacts, it added.

blocks.text: Other First Nations in the area have also voiced worries about the derailment, including Kitselas and Kitsumkalum.
Kitselas First Nation leadership said it has reached out to CN Rail directly, saying it is "deeply concerned" about the reports that diesel fuel has leaked into the Skeena River.

"The Skeena is a vital lifeline for our community and a major migratory corridor for all wild salmon and other critical aquatic species on the lower river system," said the band council in a statement.
Both Kitsumkalum and Kitselas leadership say they remain in contact with CN and continue to monitor the situation closely.
